conflicts.fact: Whether the reciprocal of an irrational number is irrational (with an exact value) — and the claim that the reciprocal of 1/√2 is irrational vs. its inclusion with a rational classification
conflicts.versions: L3 and L7 state the reciprocal of an irrational number is always irrational; L5 gives reciprocal of √2 as √2/2, consistent; L6 says irrational reciprocals cannot be expressed exactly. These are consistent, but L3 Observe lists √4 as an example from the rational set while L3 Overview says irrational slice sizes are √2 and π/4 — no conflict. (Not a true contradiction.)

conflicts.fact: Pizza B / irrational slice: what the 0.7071 figure and the 3-slice pizza represent
conflicts.versions: L1 and L2 say the 3-slice pizza gives 1/3 = 0.3333… (repeating, rational) and separately √2÷2 ≈ 0.7071 is irrational; L1 says the 3-slice arc length 'never ends and never repeats' (as an irrational) while also saying each share is 1/3 which repeats. L3 describes Pizza B as arc length √2/2 'of the radius' and also 'approximately 0.7071 of the pizza'; L4 says the √2 is the diagonal of a square with side equal to radius, and Pizza C chord for a 28 cm diameter pizza cut into 4 parts; L6 says the tile-cutting 0.7071 is the reciprocal of √2. The source of √2/2 is described inconsistently (arc length vs. radius fraction vs. chord vs. fraction of whole pizza).

conflicts.fact: Number of lessons in the sub-strand / how long the DQB and models run
conflicts.versions: L1 says the DQB stays up for all 8 lessons and the map will be revised for 8 lessons; L2, L3, L7 say 7 lessons (by Lesson 7); L7 is described as the final lesson.

conflicts.fact: Name and form of the cumulative model and DQB column labels
conflicts.versions: L1: Personal Number Classification Map and DQB columns NOTICE/WONDER/THINK WE KNOW; L2: group Number World Map and DQB columns PREDICTED/LEARNED/WONDER; L3: Pizza Model Booklet 'begun in Lesson 1' and columns We Now Know/We Still Wonder; L4: Cumulative Pizza Model; L5: Real Numbers Model. L3's booklet 'begun in Lesson 1' contradicts L1, in which the model begun is a whole-number classification map.

conflicts.fact: Order of lessons: when rational/irrational classification was taught
conflicts.versions: L3 says 'Because we know whether a number is rational or irrational (Lesson 2)' and 'Last lesson we placed these numbers on a number line'; but L2 covers odd/even/prime/composite and L4 is where rational/irrational classification and number-line placement occur.

conflicts.fact: Sequence of reciprocal teaching: reciprocal introduced as new in L5 after L3 already taught it
conflicts.versions: L3 teaches reciprocals fully (division, tables, calculators, irrational reciprocals); L5 'introduces' reciprocals as new ('first computational tool'), pretends the concept is being constructed for the first time, and refers to 'division rule we discussed in earlier lessons about rational numbers'.

conflicts.fact: Reciprocal of √2 and whether √4 is irrational / accuracy of tables
conflicts.versions: L3 Observe lists √4 (=2) among numbers while L3 overview lists irrational slice sizes; L6 Scenario B calls dividing by √4 one 'whose reciprocal is irrational' yet it equals 2 and is rational; L6 says tables reliable up to 4-digit rational values, while L3 uses tables for irrational values too.

conflicts.fact: Rational examples of slices and whether 1/3 is a 'neat' fraction
conflicts.versions: L1 says 3 slices produce a 'messy' non-terminating decimal and that decimal expansion is unlike clean fractions; L7 lists 1/3 among rational-fraction slices alongside 1/4 and 1/8 as 'neat' and says non-terminating non-repeating are irrational, whereas L1 frames 1/3's never-ending decimal as the puzzle.
